# The Problem

Package authors need to follow references across files, check imported
functions, and keep documentation consistent with their code. Language servers
help with these tasks through completion, hover information, signature help,
navigation, symbol renaming, and call hierarchy. These features help developers
catch errors while editing and make changes across a package.

There are three language servers for R:
[languageserver](https://github.com/REditorSupport/languageserver),
[Ark](https://github.com/posit-dev/ark), and Arity. languageserver is a mature R
package that runs in an R session. Ark embeds its language server in an R kernel
and powers R support in Positron. Arity, meanwhile, is a standalone language
server that works without an R session or Jupyter kernel. Adapting Ark to
Arity's design would have required extracting the server and replacing its
dependencies on the R runtime, which is what motivated the development of Arity.

Arity still has limitations that affect package development. It can misinterpret
shared roxygen documentation, miss undocumented parameters, and handle
references and call hierarchy inconsistently. Renaming can also produce invalid
R syntax, for example when a function is used as an infix operator.

Arity also needs better support for dependencies that are not installed locally.
It already provides function signatures and help for installed packages, but for
other packages it has access only to exported names. Developers therefore need
to install their dependencies to get signatures and help in the editor. Richer
metadata would remove this requirement. The editor and command-line interface
(CLI) also need to use the same cached metadata when downloads are disabled.

These improvements will help package authors and contributors catch errors
before they reach users. Publishing the metadata separately will also let other
R tools use it, while the tests and reported limitations will help their
developers evaluate similar behavior.
